p: In the year two hundred and twenty-one before Christ, three years before Hannibal set out to cross the Alps against Rome, a king named Ying Zheng, ruler of the western Chinese state of Qin, completed the conquest of the last of his rivals and became master of all China. The Chinese world had been divided for more than two centuries, an age so bloody that Chinese historians call it the Warring States. Ying Zheng, considering that the title of king was beneath his achievement, invented a new one, Huangdi, which is usually translated as emperor, and called himself Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor of Qin. He intended that his successors should be the Second Emperor, the Third, and so on for ten thousand generations. His dynasty lasted fifteen years. Yet the empire he made has lasted, with interruptions, until my own day, and the very name of China is thought to come from the name of his state.

The First Emperor and his chief minister, Li Si, followed the doctrines of a school of thinkers called the Legalists, who held that men are naturally selfish and must be governed by clear laws, severe punishments and generous rewards, and who despised the Confucian appeal to moral example as sentimental. With Legalist thoroughness, they set about making the conquered states into a single country. They abolished the old feudal nobility and divided the empire into provinces governed by officials appointed from the capital, who could be dismissed at will. They standardised the written characters, which had varied from state to state, so that a document written in the capital could be read in every province. This was, I think, the most lasting of all their works, for the unity of the Chinese writing has held together a people speaking many different tongues for two thousand years. They standardised weights and measures, coinage, and even the width of the axles of carts, so that every cart would fit the ruts of every road. They built roads and canals across the empire.

They were also, by every account, savage. In two hundred and thirteen, the story goes, the emperor ordered the burning of all books except those on medicine, divination and farming, and the histories of the state of Qin, so that scholars could not use the past to criticise the present. In the following year, it is said, he had several hundred scholars buried alive. The Encyclopaedia notes that these stories come from historians of the next dynasty, who had every reason to blacken his name, and some modern scholars doubt the details. But no one doubts that the regime was harsh.

The northern frontier of China faces the grasslands of Mongolia, home of nomadic horsemen who raided the farms and towns of the Chinese, and whom the Chinese could rarely defeat on their own ground. The warring states of the north had built walls of rammed earth against them. The First Emperor joined and extended these into a single long line of defence, at enormous cost in labour. His general Meng Tian is said to have commanded three hundred thousand men in the work, and legend tells of the countless labourers who died and were buried in the wall itself.

I must here correct a common error, of which I was myself guilty until the pages from the future set me right. The Great Wall which travellers see today, the magnificent wall of stone and brick that runs over the mountains north of Peking with its watchtowers, is not the wall of the First Emperor. It was built mostly by the Ming dynasty, in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries after Christ, long after his time. His wall, of rammed earth, has largely crumbled away. Nor is there one Great Wall, but many, built by many dynasties along different lines, which the Encyclopaedia, citing a survey of the Chinese government in the twenty-first century, reckons together at more than twenty thousand kilometres, that is some thirteen thousand miles. And I must disappoint you on one more point. It is often said that the Great Wall is the only work of man visible from the moon. The men of the future have been to the moon, and report that it is not.

As a barrier, the wall was imperfect. Determined invaders went round it or through it, and the Mongols in the thirteenth century and the Manchus in the seventeenth conquered all China in spite of it; the Manchus, indeed, were let in through a gate by a Chinese general. But as a system of watchtowers, signal fires, garrisons and controlled passes, it did much to slow raids, to channel trade, and to mark the boundary between the world of the farmer and the world of the herdsman. It is, above all, a statement: that here civilisation ends, and here we shall defend it.

The First Emperor, who feared death above all things and sent expeditions across the sea to find the elixir of immortality, died in two hundred and ten, on a journey, and his ministers concealed his death for some time by carrying his body in his carriage with a cart of rotting fish behind it to disguise the smell. He was buried near his capital, Xianyang, in a vast tomb mound. In nineteen seventy-four, farmers digging a well nearby found fragments of a clay figure. They had found the first of an army: some eight thousand life-sized soldiers of terracotta, each with an individual face, with horses and chariots, drawn up in battle order to guard their emperor in death. The tomb itself has not been opened. The historian Sima Qian, writing a century after the emperor's death, said that it contains a model of the empire with rivers of mercury. The men of the future have measured unusual quantities of mercury in the soil of the mound, and have decided, with a prudence I commend, to leave it alone.
